newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW- Internet gives life to the old and new.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW- Internet gives life to the old and new.

text.p: The Internet is giving a new lease of life to old technologies while spawning new ones, a senior Digital Equipment Corp official said on on Thursday.

"Five years ago, a lot of users were being told that if they were going to use modern technologies, they were going to have to throw away legacy applications and legacy systems like mainframes," said Bobby Choonavala.

"But the Internet has given a new lease of life to existing investments users have made," Choonavala, Digital's president for Asia Pacific operations, told Reuters in an interview at the Asia Telecom 97 trade fair.
Instead of spending huge sums of money to replace "old fashioned" systems, businesses can now spend a reasonable amount of money to introduce Internet technologies into their operations, he said.
Choonavala said many new technologies being developed now rely on and are supported by existing systems and applications, especially the Internet.
Among them was the concept of the network computer (NC).
"NCs could be another tool. It is a simple, inexpensive way to access the Internet and intranet," he said.
The NC is a barebone appliance with no real memory, operating system or resident software. It gets all its programming and applications off a network like the Internet.
Digital has developed a prototype of the NC with its StrongArm chip.

It believed new tools like the NC were likely to take off among businesses first as they have access to their own intranets, but Choonavala said the NC would be used in homes through cheaper set-top boxes, handheld devices and even watches as the technology became more pervasive and attracted more applications.
Researchers like Zona Research have projected 11 million NCs will be shipped in 1998 and 78 million in 2000.
Choonavala said while there appeared to be competing ideas in the age of the fast infiltrating Internet and deregulation in key sectors like telecommunications, there was room for all.

"The market place will decide which one they want to go with. I believe at the end of the day, there is enough space for every technology. It is like GSM (Global System for Mobile Communications) and CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access) in mobile phones)," he said.

Choonavala said the twin forces of the Internet and deregulation were compelling companies to seek alliances and partnerships as no single company could provide all the solutions and services, with individual companies focusing on their own strengths.
Digital itself has alliances with Oracle, Microsoft and also with telecoms companies like British Telecom .
In its latest alliance, Digital has teamed with Ericsson, Oracle and Acorn ACN.L to offer a system to select and view news, movies, information and educational programs using Internet technology.
